links.reason: Both verses call on the grove's heron as the one witness of the man's conduct: Ainthinai Aimpathu 45 asks மன்ற விடுவனவோ ... குருகு, and Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62 asks கொடுமை அறியாகொல் ... கண்டும் ... குருகு. These are not incompatible claims; both treat the bird as a witness, so the pair is a shared image. The teaches sentence builds one story of trust collapsing across two poems by different poets, which neither poem states.

The only link is the word எஃகு: in 759 wealth is the steel that cuts the foe's pride (செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகு), in 773 help to a fallen foe is valour's edge (ஊராண்மை மற்றதன் எஃகு). The two make no claims about the same thing, so there is no tension. 'Cutting and sparing are both called sharpness' only restates the shared word.

Clouds rising like elephants is a stock image, but the two do differ: Kar Narpathu 12 makes it an omen (ஐயந்தீர் காட்சி, rising வலம்), while Natrinai 237 likens the clouds to the elephants Andiran gathered for suppliants (இரவலர் ... புரவு எதிர்ந்து தொகுத்த யானை). The contrast in the teaches sentence is true, though 'a gift laid up for those who wait' reads more into the simile than உலகம் உவப்ப gives.

The word இளிவரவு does echo the Kural's இளிவந்தது. But இல்லது நோக்கி, இளிவரவு கூறாமுன், நல்லது வெஃகி, வினை செய்வார் reads most simply as giving to those in want before they are shamed into asking, not as bathers keeping their own requests out of prayer. The note and the teaches sentence rest on that stretched reading of an obscure festival catalogue.

Thinaimozhi 33 opens with the friendship ethic itself, கடையாயார் நட்பேபோல் ... இளநலம் உண்டாய், the base friend who stays while there is profit, which is what Kural 812 describes (உறின்நட்டு அறின்ஒரூஉம்). The couplet ends in a shrug (பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்?), and the wife whose youth was consumed cannot take that stance. So the qualification is real and specific.

A newly calved buffalo cow with her calf is a stock marutham town epithet. In Ainkurunuru 92 it belongs to her father's town (நுந்தை நும்மூர்), not to a home the suitor offers. In Kuruntokai 181 it is part of the ஊரன் epithet, not an emblem the wife makes of her own worn-out home. The teaches sentence's courtship-to-karpu arc is built on top of a shared stock image.

The shared word நிறை is real: the Kural's desire breaks the door of restraint (நிறையென்னும் ... கதவு), and Paripadal 6 likens the flood to lovers of one desire breaking the restraint of the heart (விருப்பு ஒன்றுபட்டவர் உளம் நிறை உடைத்தென). But in the Paripadal the broken restraint is only the vehicle of a simile for the river. The drum that sounds (அறைக எனும் உரைச் சிறைப் பறை) need not be a celebration, so 'a public and welcome release' overreads.
links.text_issue: line 14 is a prose heading, not verse

links.reason: Both call wealth impermanent in matching words: the Kural's அற்கா இயல்பிற்றுச் செல்வம and Natrinai 46's மன்னாப் பொருள். The Kural turns this into an instruction for when wealth is got (பெற்றால் ... ஆங்கே செயல்), while the friend uses it, together with youth passing like an arrow's shadow, against going after wealth at all. One premise yields opposite conclusions, which neither verse shows alone.

Akananuru 317 does quote the promise as a description of the season (வருவேம் என்ற பருவம்), and he comes. Ainkurunuru 350 has the season of his assurance come without him (அவரோ வாரார் தான்வந்தன்றே ... அவர்த் தெளிக்கும் பொழுதே). The kept-against-broken contrast is real, but 'the same signs' overstates: 350 names the neem, which is not in 317's catalogue.

In both the friend reads the season: in Natrinai 86 the late-dew flowers fix that the men came early (முற்றா வேனில் முன்னி வந்தோரே), and in 99 she calls the flowers foolish (மடவ ஆகலின் மலர்ந்தன) in order to comfort. That her reading follows the man's conduct is a fair point. But in 86 the man has actually come, by its thurai, so the flowers there are not an argument made for the woman, and the generalization goes beyond the pair.

Both rank a woman's body as a weapon: the Kural's look holds death (கூற்றமோ), while Ainkurunuru 361 climbs from the eyes to fiercer breasts and fiercer shoulders (கண்ணினும் கதவநின் முலையே). The reversal of the eye's primacy is a real and specific contrast. 'Half joking against grave' is an impression; the Kural's question is just as hyperbolic.

Kuruntokai 323 counts as lived only the days spent sleeping on her shoulders (தோளிணைத் துஞ்சிக் கழிந்த நாள் ... வாழு நாளே) and calls the rest பதடி வைகல். Kural 1103 sets the same sleep on soft shoulders (மென்றோள் துயில்) against the lotus-eyed one's world. The pair moves the ranking from heaven against embrace to which days of a life count, which is specific and true.

Both mark the wedding: Ainkurunuru 230 lists the harm (மெல்தோள் நெகிழவும் திருநுதல் பசப்பவும்) beside அயர்வர்நன் மணனே, and Natrinai 386 recalls him coming with the word வதுவை. That is the shared topic. Reading 230 as 'payment of what he owed' is not in the Tamil, and 386's colophon places the poem after a parathai episode, which the note ignores.

The link rests on one attribute, incomparability: the Kural's தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான் is the god whose feet end anxiety, and Patitruppattu 73's பிறர்உவமம் ஆகா is a king. The poet's distress (வருந்துவல் யானே) is that hearers do not believe his praise, not the mind's anxiety (மனக்கவலை) of Kural 7. The teaches sentence joins two unrelated sorrows through a shared epithet.

Both liken the girl to Kuttuvan's Thondi: the man's praise in Ainkurunuru 178 (குட்டுவன் தொண்டி யன்ன), and in Akananuru 290 her eyes, which have lost the beauty of Thondi's neythal (தொண்டி முன்துறை ... நெய்தல் மணிஏர் மாண்நலம் ஒரீஇ) before marriage (மணவா முன்னும்). The puram place-name moves from praise to a measure of loss, which the note states accurately. The reference to poems 179 and 180 goes outside the packet.

Both measure a woman's beauty by Kuttuvan's Maranthai (மரந்தை அன்ன இவள் நலம் / மரந்தை அன்னஎன் நலம்). The courtesan of Akananuru 376 demands it back as he leaves (நலம்தந்து சென்மே). Natrinai 35 has it slacken though he never leaves her side (உழையின் போகாது அளிப்பினும் ... ஞெகிழ்ந்த கவின்), putting the cause in love itself. Opposite causes under one civic simile is a specific lesson.

The rope-breaking buffalo is a real and distinctive shared image (கயிறுபரிந்து / நோன் தளை பரிந்து). But Ainkurunuru 95 names no straying at all: it says only படர்மலி அருநோய் செய்தனன் எமக்கே. So the claim that the image was already a fixed sign of the straying lord assumes the very reading it is meant to prove.

Thiraiyan really is named in both: the idyll's திரைதரு மரபின் உரவோன் உம்பல் ... பல்வேற் றிரையன், and Akananuru 340's பொலம்பூண் திரையன் பல்பூங் கானற் பவத்திரி. But the idyll's line is a genealogy playing on the name, not a statement that he rules a coast, and the two Thiraiyans are assumed to be one. The teaches sentence's claim about a shared identity goes beyond the lines given.

In Kuruntokai 25 the only witness of the union is a heron watching for aaral fish (யாரும் இல்லை ... குருகும் உண்டு), and she says யானெவன் செய்கோ. Kainnilai 50 refuses to speak to him or to the anril and addresses only the stork that saw the oath (கடுஞ்சூளில் தான்கண்டு ... நாராய் கேள்). The move of the bird witness from proof of helplessness to the one hearer is accurate and specific.

The epithets match closely: the Kural's மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் and the Neelakesi's தண்டாமரைமேல் நடந்தான். The Neelakesi stanza excuses itself against the old Agama (பண்டு ஆகமத்துள் பயிலா உரை), so the lotus-walker there is the poet's own Jain lord. The pair shows the epithet in use in that tradition.

Both turn on a stag's care, and the deer differ. Kuruntokai 213 has the stag stand as shade for its fawn (மறிக்குநிழல் ஆகி), by hearsay (என்ப), as proof of his love. Akananuru 34 has the stag feed its doe and guard her sleep (மடப்பிணை அருத்தி ... துஞ்சுபுறம் காக்கும்), moving the returning man. Calling them 'two ends of one iraicchi' overstates two independent poems, but the promise-and-sight contrast holds.

Both face the town's gossip (அலர்). Kural 1149 cancels the shame of gossip once he has left (அலர்நாண ஒல்வதோ). Natrinai 116 has the bond burst like a fallen jackfruit while the town's women, not knowing, keep up their talk (அறியாது ... இன்னும் ஓவார் என் திறத்து அலரே). The contrast is real but thin. Natrinai 116's thurai is a delayed marriage, not desertion.

In Natrinai 161 the returning man wonders whether the omen birds have already told her (நம் வரவினைப் புள் அறிவுறீஇயினகொல்லோ). In Natrinai 169 he addresses the house lizard as if he could make it sound for her (படும்கொல் வாழி நெடுஞ் சுவர்ப் பல்லி). The move from imagining her omen to wishing he could send one is specific and accurate.

Akananuru 242 calls the diviner அறியா வேலன். Natrinai 34 tells Murugan he came to the veri knowing the sickness was not his seizure (நின் அணங்கு அன்மை அறிந்தும் ... வந்தோய்) and calls him a fool (மடவை மன்ற). The scorn moving from an ignorant priest to a knowing god is exactly what the two texts show.

The shared image of mullai buds as teeth is real: Kar Narpathu 14 has முல்லை இலங்கெயிறு ஈன and the cloud laughing (நகும), and Kuruntokai 220 has buds opening like a wild cat smiling (வெருகுசிரித் தன்ன). The two make no incompatible claim, though: one says he will come, the other that he has not yet, so this is not a tension. The வெருகு simile describes the buds' shape and does not make the season sneer, so 'mockery' is read in.

Both describe the Parankunram crowd: Maduraikkanchi counts it as one sound of the marutham land (தண்பரங் குன்றிற் கலிகொள் சும்மை), and Paripadal 17 makes it the hill's beauty (அனைய, பரங்குன்றின் அணி). The difference is true, but it is mostly the difference between a city catalogue and a hymn. 'Became, in the devotional songs' implies a historical change that the pair cannot show.

Both have spears and elephants, but Kalavazhi 23 is a simile of elephants rising from blood like clouds in a red sky (செக்கர்கொள் வானிற் கருங்கொண்மூப் போன்றவே) on Chempiyan's field. It says nothing of the warrior's ethic, and the Kural's laugh while plucking his own wound (மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்) has no counterpart. 'Credits it to the king' is just the series' closing formula.

Kural 552 condemns the levy beyond due as robbery (வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென் றதுபோலும்). Purananuru 184 argues from yield, with the elephant fed by measured balls against one let loose in a field, ending தானும் உண்ணான், உலகமும் கெடுமே. The moral against prudential grounding of the same rule is accurate and specific.

Akananuru 80 refuses the night and invites a day meeting (புன்னைஅம் கானல், பகல்வந் தீமே). Thinaimalai 35 forbids the night and warns of gossip by day (பகல்வரின் ... கவ்வையாம்). That contrast is real. 'A later stage' and 'the only road left is marriage' are not in either poem, and Thinaimalai 35's text is uncertain.
links.text_issue: site prints a different verse 35; சுலா அகற்றி, மார்க் obscure

links.reason: The exact phrase பாலும் உண்ணாள் opens the symptom in both. In Akananuru 48 it is the foster mother's question, which the friend answers by disclosure (அறத்தொடு நின்றது). In Kuruntokai 396 the foster mother reads it only after the girl has gone (அவனொடு செலவே). Placing the same symptom before disclosure and after elopement is specific. 'Decides which follows' is a slight overgeneralization.

The poet is the same per both colophons, and Kuruntokai 91's frontier town at night (கொன்முனை இரவூர்) fears the generous-handed chariot lord (ஓவாது ஈயும் மாரி வண்கை ... அஞ்சி), Anji, the subject of Purananuru 97's threat. The wife's sleepless marriage measured by the terror puram praise creates is a real and specific use. அஞ்சி may be both the name and 'fearing', but either way the fear is of that lord.

Purananuru 182 says the world stands on men who would give their lives for fame (புகழ்எனின், உயிருங் கொடுக்குவர்). Natrinai 115 says the lover would not stay away even for endless fame (நன் புகழ் உலப்பு இன்று பெறினும் தவிரலர்). These are not incompatible: love above fame and fame above life can both hold. So the pair at most qualifies the heroic scale; it does not overturn it.

Ainkurunuru 66 accuses the rival of snatching even his coming home to the toddling son (தளர்நடைப் புதல்வனை உள்ளி ... வருதலும் வௌவியோள்). Akananuru 16 shows a courtesan taking that son to her breast in the chariot street (வருக மாள, என் உயிர்). The son as the point the rival reaches for from both sides is accurate and specific.

Both are courtesans answering reported slander (எற்புறங் கூறும் என்ப / கழறுப என்ப). But Akananuru 76's answer is a resolve to seize and hold him as the Kaveri held Atti (கொண்டுகை வலித்தல் சூழ்ந்திசின்), not a public contest announced in the town. The 'convention of a public contest' fits only Kuruntokai 364's thunangai.

The wording is close: Kalittokai 14's செம்மையின் இகந்து ஒரீஇப் பொருள் and Kural 113's நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம். The Kural concedes 'even if it brings good' (நன்றே தரினும) and still says to give it up, while the poem denies any good in either world (இம்மையும் மறுமையும் பகை ஆவது). The qualification is precise.

The half-line is verbatim apart from the lamp: பாவை விளக்கிற் பரூஉச்சுட ரழல in the wife's room in Mullaippattu 85, and பாண்டில் விளக்கிற் பரூஉச்சுட ரழல on the king's round to see the wounded (விழுப்புண் காணிய புறம்போந்து) in Nedunalvadai. A formula of the night vigil set on opposite sides of a separation is a meaningful shared image.

The words are set against each other: 371's அறநெறி இதுவெனத் தெளிந்த and 376's அறனில் பால். But 371 reports what the girl judged, not a concession by the mother, and 376 blames fate, not the girl's choice. So the two claims are about different things, and the tension holds only loosely. 'Inside a single lament' is also inexact for two separate poems of a decade.

Kuruntokai 212's chariot comes only to be seen and leaves shame (காண வந்து நாணப் பெயரும்). Kuruntokai 311's chariot that would not stop was seen by all the girls (ஆயம் எல்லாம் உடன்கண் டன்றே), and so the gossip. 212 already ties the visible visit to shame, so the pair adds little beyond the shared shore convention.

Kuruntokai 218 lines 1 to 4 are negative: கடனும் பூணாம், கைந்நூல் யாவாம், புள்ளும் ஓராம், விரிச்சியும் நில்லாம், உள்ளலும் உள்ளாம். She will not make vows, tie threads, heed birds or wait on omens, nor even think of him. The note and the teaches sentence read these as rites she performs and thoughts she keeps, so 'a life kept busy with ritual' inverts the poem. The real parallel is உயிர்க்குயிர் அன்னர் against the Kural's வேறல்லம் என்பார்.

Both use மதில் பொரூஉம். Kalittokai 67 says the walled town has known no siege but the Vaiyai's beating on its wall (மதில் பொரூஉம் பகை அல்லால் நேராதார் போர் முற்று ஒன்று அறியாத). Paripadal 12 shows the town, at news that the Vaiyai comes beating on Madurai's wall, dressing and riding out to meet it. The flood as the city's one welcomed assault is accurate and specific.

The two belong to different books and poets, and the animals differ: Thinaimalai 1 asks after an arrow-struck deer (ஏமரை), while Thinaimozhi 8 denies that a bleeding tusker came (குருதி ஒழுக ... களிறு). They share only the conventional hunter's pretext, so 'one exchange' across two books is invented.
links.text_issue: Thinaimalai 1 not found on the comparison site

links.reason: Ainkurunuru 47 charges that the man lies like his bard (நின் பாணன் போலப் பலபொய்த்தல்). Paripadal 18 confronts the bard with the marks on the man and calls his song a bloom of lies (பொய் வளம் பூத்தன, பாணா! நின் பாட்டு). The lying bard of marutham is a shared convention. That the god's hill is a place where straying was caught is something the Paripadal shows by itself.

Both use the elephant pair of the cool rains to mark the season: in Kar Narpathu 38 the bull plays with his mate (பிடியோ டிசைந்தாடும்) and he has not come, and in Akananuru 85 the bull feeds his mate's calf (கன்றுபசி களைஇய ... ஊட்டும்) as the promised season. The teaches sentence itself says the image carries the same sense in both, so there is no incompatible claim, only one image with two verdicts.

poems.note: The stag sleeping in the thin shade the elephant left acts, but no one-sentence sense for the lovers follows from it.

The dog pair could be read as an iraicchi carrier, but the hunt, the starving teatless mate and her faithful nature map part by part onto the journey for wealth and the waiting wife, so it is ullurai.
Every image is joined openly to the heroine or the man (போல், ஒத்தி), so there is no hidden comparison.
A puram (kaanchi) poem, so both fields are null.
Lines 1 and 2 are obscure; the ripening millet that ends the trysts is said openly, with போல் beside it.
The verse is corrupt or obscure in lines 1 and 2, and the similes that follow are open.
The birds' paired life is the whole of the poem and its message is spoken outright, so striking them leaves nothing.
Each bull's charge is likened openly with போன்ம், and taming the bull as the way to win the girl is said in lines 36 to 38.

iraicchi.act: The stork that went to see the heron's dead chick grieves more than the heron itself.
iraicchi.sense: Even a stork feels another's loss more than the one bereaved, so the man should feel her distress and embrace her more than before.

poems.note: Whether செத்தென means the chick died or the stork mistook it is uncertain; the act of grief for another stands either way.

iraicchi.act: The little white bird, its back soaked by the spray, dwells shivering and suffering in the cold of the shore grove.
iraicchi.sense: As the bird endures the cold where it lives, she has nothing left to lose but her life if the shore lord leaves her.

poems.note: This is borderline under condition 2: பனிபுலந்து உறையும் is read as an act of enduring, not only a look.
The fish snatching the fallen mango may suggest easy pleasure, but no second correspondence with the oath against the wife's charge can be named.
The crow that called the guest is the poem's subject; strike it and the poem's sense goes.
All the likenesses are open (புரையும், அன்ன).
The bee that leaves the flooded lotus and returns maps well onto the straying man, but it is openly likened to citizens who flee and come back (குடி போல), so it fails condition 2 as written.
The text of lines 2 and 3 is corrupt.
The monkey pair acts as one, but the troop as kin, the secret union and the tidying of the hair to hide its traces map part by part, so it is ullurai.
